Could there be moments where you allow yourself to step back while still being attentive to their needs?

Calmer? Oh, no. God, no. It was the opposite of calm. It was agonizing. My heart was just hammering the whole time, and I felt... stretched. Like a rubber band about to snap.

But more in control? Yes. In a strange way, yes. I couldn't control the headache, of course. But I was controlling what I *could* control, which was my own attention. I was doing my job. To just walk away and not watch... that would have felt like absolute chaos. That would have felt like I was completely out of control of the situation.

Counselor: It sounds like the experience of being vigilant brings a sense of control for you, even though it feels physically and emotionally overwhelming. What do you think it would mean to acknowledge that feeling in control doesn't necessarily equate to being on high alert all the time? How might you explore finding a balance between being attentive to your loved ones and allowing yourself moments of respite, so that you can manage the tension you're feeling?

What did it prevent... I... well, nothing happened on Tuesday, so I suppose it didn't prevent anything from happening to *him*. I know that sounds strange.

But it prevented me from being caught off guard. It prevented the shock. If he *had* suddenly started to look confused or slumped over, I would have been there. It prevented me from having that split second of blissful ignorance before the horror hits. I just... I can't be surprised by something like that ever again. That's the real thing it prevents.

Counselor: It sounds like your vigilance serves as a protective mechanism to shield you from the shock and fear of unexpected situations, which makes sense given the stakes you're facing. What do you think it would be like to explore the notion that being prepared doesn't always have to come from a place of constant alertness? How might you examine the idea that being present can also mean being open to experiencing life without the burden of fear, while still being attentive to your husband's needs?

It makes me feel... broken, I guess. It makes me feel like a bad mom, that I chose to watch my husband sleep instead of listening to my son.

But the alternative... the idea of being relaxed and happy and then getting hit by that... that freight train of horror... again. That feels so much worse. It's like, I can either have this constant, low-grade pain of being on guard, or I can risk the absolute, soul-destroying agony of being blindsided.

When you put it like that, it's a terrible exchange. But it feels like the only one I can possibly make.

Counselor: It sounds like you're feeling a deep sense of conflict between your responsibilities as a caregiver and the fear of being caught off guard by unexpected events. What do you think it would mean to explore the idea that being present with your son doesn't diminish your ability to care for your husband? How might you begin to challenge the belief that you must choose between constant vigilance and enjoying moments with your family?

I... I honestly don't know what that would even look like, Dr. Anya. It sounds... peaceful. But I can't imagine it.

In my mind, the dread *is* the switch that turns on the preparedness. They're all tangled up together. If I'm not feeling that horrible, sick feeling in my stomach, how would I know I was being vigilant enough?

It feels like asking me to be a good guard dog, but without letting me bark. The feeling of dread is the only thing that proves to me that I'm actually on duty.

Counselor: It sounds like you're deeply connected to the feeling of dread as a way to gauge your vigilance and sense of duty, which makes sense given the circumstances you’re facing. What do you think it might be like to explore alternative ways to signal to yourself that you're being attentive, without relying solely on that feeling of dread? Could there be other cues or practices you could consider that might help you feel prepared while also allowing for a sense of peace?

I... I guess it means that part of me knows what to do, even when I'm not in a full-blown panic. I'd still be a good wife, I'd still take care of him.

But... that was for a headache. That's an easy action to take. What about for something else, something subtle? I worry that if I'm just 'concerned,' I won't have the... the urgency... to act fast enough if it's really, really bad.

The dread feels like fuel. It's awful, but it makes me feel like I could lift a car if I had to. 'Concern' just feels... so quiet and polite. I'm not sure it would be enough when it really matters.

Counselor: It sounds like you're recognizing that there is a part of you that knows how to respond even when you're not in a heightened state of panic, which is an important realization. What do you think it would look like to trust that inner knowledge while also allowing for a more balanced state of concern? How might you explore ways to cultivate that sense of readiness without relying solely on dread as your motivator?

A time I had to act quickly... oh, let me think. It's hard to remember anything but the panic lately.

Oh... yes. When my daughter, Clara, was about six. We were at the park and she fell from the top of the jungle gym. The sound her arm made when she landed... I'll never forget it.

And I... I didn't feel dread then. Not like on Tuesday. It was... something else. Just pure, cold adrenaline. I didn't think, I just ran. I scooped her up, held her arm still, and everything got very sharp and very quiet in my head. I got her and Erik into the car and drove to the hospital, and I was completely calm on the outside.

The dread came later. Sitting in the waiting room while they did the x-rays, that's when my mind started screaming. What if she'd hit her head? What if I hadn't been watching closely enough? What if it was my fault? The shaking and the terror... that didn't start until after she was already being taken care of. It's strange, I hadn't thought of that.

Counselor: It sounds like you were able to tap into a different kind of response in that moment with Clara, one that allowed you to act decisively and calmly despite the circumstances. What do you think it reveals about your capability to respond effectively even without the presence of dread? How might you explore the possibility of accessing that same clarity and focus in other situations, while also allowing yourself to feel more at ease?

I... I don't know what to make of that, Dr. Anya. I've never thought of it that way before.

It's true. When Clara was hurt, it was so clear, so immediate. I could *see* the problem. There was no time for anything but action.

But with Lars's headache... it's an invisible threat. It's silent. The dread feels like the only thing that alerts me that there might be something terrible happening under the surface. It feels... necessary for that kind of danger.

But... yes. It is strange. The real emergency had no dread, and the what-if emergency had all of it. I'm... I'm not sure what that means.

Counselor: It sounds like you’re grappling with the difference between visible emergencies and the silent, insidious threats that create so much fear. What do you think it might mean for you to recognize that your ability to respond effectively can exist even in the absence of dread? How could you begin to explore other ways to assess potential threats that might allow you to feel more grounded and less burdened by anxiety?

I... I don't know. I'm trying to wrap my head around it.

Maybe... maybe the dread isn't meant for the moment of crisis. Maybe its purpose is for the time *before*. With Clara, there was no 'before,' it just happened. But with an illness... that's a slow, creeping danger. The dread is what keeps me searching for it, I think. It's the alarm for the danger you can't see yet. It feels like it's trying to... to prevent the 'before' from becoming an 'after'.

Counselor: It sounds like you're beginning to see the role of dread as a kind of early warning system for potential threats, especially with ongoing illnesses. What do you think it would look like to acknowledge that function of dread while also exploring other ways to stay vigilant without it becoming overwhelming? How might you create space for both awareness of potential issues and the ability to enjoy the present moment with your family?

A more balanced statement... okay. I'm trying to think. Maybe something like... 'My fear is telling me this is a tumor because of his history, but it's also very possible it's just a headache from his stressful day and dehydration.'

But, Dr. Anya, even as I say that, my mind just adds a 'yes, but...' at the end. It's like my fear immediately argues back, 'Yes, but what if you're wrong? What if you relax and you miss it?' It feels... so flimsy. Is that the kind of thing you mean, though?

Counselor: It sounds like you’re beginning to recognize the tension between your fears and a more balanced perspective, which is an important step. What do you think might help you to challenge that "yes, but..." response when it arises? How could you explore the evidence for both sides of that thought, and what might be a way to strengthen your belief in the possibility that it could just be a simple headache?

If I could have believed it, even just a little? I... I'm not sure. But if I could... maybe the feeling in my chest wouldn't have been so tight. The dread would still have been there, I'm sure of it, but maybe it would have been... a lower hum instead of a scream.

Maybe I could have actually registered the words on the page of my book. And... oh, God... when Erik came in to talk to me, maybe I could have looked up and really seen him. Maybe I wouldn't have felt so miles away. That part makes me feel awful to think about.

Counselor: It sounds like you're experiencing a deep sense of loss in those moments when you're unable to fully engage with the present due to the overwhelming dread. A Thought Record... okay. Yes, I'm... I'm open to hearing about it.

I'm just a little nervous, I guess. It sounds... official. I'm worried it'll be another thing on my list that I won't do perfectly. My days are just so packed, between the kids and the house... I'm just not sure I'll do it right. Sorry, I don't mean to sound ungrateful. I do want to try.

Counselor: It sounds like you're feeling a mix of openness to the Thought Record and some apprehension about adding another task to your already busy life. Okay. Just one... yes. That sounds... that sounds more manageable. Less like a big final exam I'm going to fail. I can try to do one.

I guess I'm just worried that when I'm in the middle of feeling that panic, I won't be able to think clearly enough to remember what I'm supposed to write down. But... okay. One. I will try to do just one. Thank you.

Counselor: It’s great to hear that you’re feeling more open to trying just one Thought Record; that sounds like a positive step forward. Yes... yes, that helps a lot, actually. The idea of trying to find the paper and think clearly while my heart is pounding out of my chest... it just seemed impossible.

But doing it after, when the storm has passed a bit... okay. I can see that. It feels more like doing detective work on something that's already happened, instead of trying to... to perform some kind of logical trick in the middle of a fire.

Okay. I will try my best to do one this week. Thank you for explaining that.

Counselor: It sounds like you’ve found a more manageable approach to using the Thought Record, which is encouraging. It was... a lot. I feel pretty wrung out, to be honest. But in a good way, maybe?

Talking about that moment with Erik, and how I just wasn't there for him... that's a heavy feeling to sit with. But when you asked about Clara and her arm... I haven't thought about that day in a long time. I'd never seen it that way before, how the dread wasn't there when something was actually happening.

So, yes. It was... it was a hard session, but a good one. It's given me a lot to think about. Thank you.

Counselor: It sounds like this session has brought up some significant reflections for you, and I appreciate your willingness to sit with those heavier feelings. Okay. Thank you again, Dr. Anya. I will... I'll try my best with the detective sheet. See you next week.

Counselor: It sounds like you’re feeling motivated to take on this new approach with the Thought Record, and that’s a positive mindset to have. Hi, Dr. Anya. Good to see you.

I've been... okay, I think. It's been an up and down week. The usual, really, my baseline anxiety has been floating around a 7, maybe a 7 and a half. It did spike up to a 9 on Wednesday night, though. Lars had a work dinner and was driving home late, and... well, my mind just went to all the worst places. I tried remembering what we talked about, but in the moment, it's like all the logic just evaporates.

Counselor: It sounds like you've been experiencing a lot of fluctuation in your anxiety levels this week, especially with the spike when Lars was out. Right... the thought record. I'm so sorry, Dr. Anya, I feel terrible about it. I did get the sheet out on Wednesday night when I was waiting for Lars. I sat down with it at the kitchen table, but... I just stared at it. My hands were shaking, and I couldn't even form a sentence.

I just *knew* it wasn't going to help. When the dread is that strong, a piece of paper isn't going to make a difference. I don't think it ever will.

Counselor: It sounds like you experienced a lot of overwhelming feelings when you tried to use the Thought Record, and it's completely understandable to feel frustrated in that moment. Okay... the situation. Right.

It was Wednesday night, about 10:15 pm. Lars was driving home from a work dinner downtown. He'd said he would be home by 10, and he... he wasn't. And it was raining. Not a storm, just that slick, misty kind of rain. He hadn't texted, he hadn't called. The house was completely quiet. That's it, really. That was the situation.

Counselor: It sounds like the situation felt particularly intense for you, especially with the combination of uncertainty and the weather. How did those specific circumstances influence your thoughts and feelings in that moment? Let’s explore together what thoughts came up for you when you noticed that Lars hadn’t returned as expected.

The thought... it wasn't even a sentence, really. It was just a flash. A picture.

I could see his car on the highway, the headlights cutting through the rain, and then another car... just sliding across the median. The sound of it, the chrome and the glass... it was so vivid. The immediate thought was, 'He's been in a wreck. He's dead.' I just knew it. It felt less like a worry and more like a... a piece of news I was just receiving. My whole body went cold.

Counselor: It sounds like that vivid image and immediate thought created a very intense emotional response for you, making it feel very real in the moment. It's completely understandable to feel that way when faced with uncertainty and fear for someone you care about. What do you think might help you to separate those intense images and feelings from the reality of the situation? How could we explore the evidence for and against that thought about Lars being in a wreck?

Dread. Just pure, ice-cold dread. It's not just a feeling in my head, Dr. Anya, it's... it's in my whole body. My stomach just drops, and I feel so completely helpless.

And terror. The feeling is so strong... it proves the thought is real, you know? It's not just an idea when your body is reacting like that. It feels like a fact.

Counselor: It sounds like the physical sensations of dread and terror can be incredibly overwhelming and feel like they validate your thoughts in those moments. It's important to recognize that our bodies can react strongly to fear, but those feelings don't always reflect reality. What do you think might be some alternative explanations for what could be happening with Lars, aside from the worst-case scenario? Let’s explore those possibilities together.

Evidence that it was true... Well, I mean... no one had called me from the hospital, so I guess I didn't have *proof* in that sense.

But the evidence *was* that he was late. He hadn't called. And Lars... he knows how I get. He *always* texts if he's going to be even five minutes late. Always. So the fact that he was silent... that felt like all the proof in the world. It was proof that something was horribly wrong, and my mind just... it filled in the blank with the only thing it could possibly be.

Counselor: It makes sense that Lars’s silence and being late would trigger such intense feelings and thoughts, especially given your past experiences. It sounds like you were relying on his usual behaviors to gauge the situation, which can sometimes lead to overgeneralization. Other reasons... I mean, I suppose... his phone could have died? Or maybe there was just bad traffic because of the rain and he got stuck behind an accident.

But he's so careful about keeping his phone charged. And even if he was in traffic, he could just use the Bluetooth in the car to call me. It would take two seconds. It... those possibilities just feel like wishful thinking, you know? They don't have the same weight as the silence. The silence felt so... loud. It felt like it meant something terrible.

Counselor: It sounds like the silence felt very heavy and significant to you, almost like it was amplifying your fears. I don't know... maybe he ran into someone from work on his way to the car, and they just stood there talking? His boss, maybe. That happens sometimes.

But still... he knows me. He knows what I'm like. It takes five seconds to send a text. The fact that he didn't do that, that's what felt so wrong. It tells me that something must have *prevented* him from doing it.

Counselor: It’s understandable to feel that Lars’s silence might indicate something serious, especially given your concerns. It sounds like you’re wrestling with both the possibility of a benign explanation and the weight of your worries. I'm trying to think... well, he does get very absorbed in his audiobooks. Or sometimes he'll get a call from his father in Denmark, and with the time difference, he always takes it. He could have been talking on the hands-free in the car and just lost all track of time. He does that. He gets totally lost in a conversation.

But... for 15 minutes past when he said he'd be home? He knows the rule. He knows I start to unravel. It just... it doesn't feel like him to just forget like that. It still feels like the only reason he wouldn't text is because he *couldn't*.

Counselor: I can see how deeply you care about Lars and how his typical behaviors shape your expectations. Well... no, I don't think so. He's always been so... so painfully aware of how I get. It's our rule.

Wait. Actually... there was one time. Last spring. He was meant to be home from work at 5:30 and he didn't show up until almost 7. No calls, no texts. I was... I was a wreck. I was picturing his car on the side of the road, the whole thing.

It turned out our elderly neighbor Mr. Henderson had fallen while trying to get his mail, and Lars had found him and helped him back inside and waited with him until his daughter could get there. His phone was on silent in his briefcase in the car.

But... that was during the day. This was late at night, on the highway, in the rain. It just felt so much more dangerous. The stakes felt higher.

Counselor: It sounds like that previous experience with Lars really highlights how much you care about him and how those feelings of worry can intensify, especially in different situations. I... well, I suppose it tells me that the feeling can be wrong. That my dread can scream 'fire' when there's no fire at all. I hear that, logically.

But, Dr. Anya... that time with Mr. Henderson was during the day. This was late at night, on the highway, in the rain. It just felt so much more... potent. The chances of something bad happening felt a million times higher.

It's like... just because the alarm was wrong last time doesn't mean it's broken for good. It just means that specific time wasn't the real danger. It feels almost reckless to ignore it the next time it goes off.

Counselor: It’s insightful that you recognize how your feelings can sometimes lead you to perceive danger, even when the situation may not warrant it. It felt like I was being electrocuted, but from the inside out. My heart was pounding so hard I could feel it in my throat. I couldn't breathe right... just these shallow little sips of air that didn't feel like enough.

And my mind... it was just a loop. The image of the crash, the sound of the metal... over and over. It's not like thinking, it's like being trapped in a movie. I just sat there, frozen, waiting for the phone to ring and confirm it all. It felt like I was already a widow.

Counselor: It sounds incredibly overwhelming to experience those intense physical sensations and racing thoughts, almost as if you're caught in a terrifying scene that you can't escape. Okay... a more balanced thought. It's so hard to make the words come out. I guess it would be something like... 'I am feeling this intense dread because he's late, and my mind is going to the worst-case scenario. But... there have been other times, like with Mr. Henderson, where I felt this exact same way and he was perfectly safe.'

But Dr. Anya, it just feels so weak. It feels like telling myself a fairy tale when I'm facing a monster. The dread feels true. The other story... it feels like a nice idea, but not a real one. What if I latch onto that thought and this is the one time the monster is real?

Counselor: It’s completely understandable to feel that way, especially when the emotions are so intense and the fear feels very real. No... of course not. If he called and said he was hurt, I would... I would have been on the phone with an ambulance in a second. I would have been out the door. The balanced thought wouldn't change that.

But... it feels like it would stop me from being ready for that call. The dread is what makes me sit by the phone, listening for it to ring. It's what keeps me... poised. Without it, I'd be... No... no, it wasn't dread. It was... just... clarity. Everything got very sharp and quiet. The danger was right there in front of me, I could see it. There was no question what I had to do.

But this... waiting for Lars... that's different. The danger is invisible. It's a ghost. The dread is what makes me believe the ghost might be real. It's what keeps me watching the shadows.

With Clara, I was reacting to something that had already happened. With Lars, the dread is... it's trying to stop it from happening in the first place. It doesn't feel like the same thing at all. I'm sorry, I'm not sure if I'm making sense.

Well... none. Of course. I know that my sitting here, feeling sick to my stomach, didn't change the traffic or make the rain stop. I know it sounds completely irrational when you say it like that.

But it... it feels like the only thing I can *do*. It's like... if I'm not standing watch, if I'm not feeling the terror on his behalf, then I've abandoned him out there. The dread... it's like a vigil. It feels like the price of love, almost. If I stop worrying, it feels like I've stopped caring and have just left him to his fate.

Counselor: It’s completely understandable to feel that way, as if your worry is a form of love and protection. I... well, I mean... I do everything for him. I make sure his favorite coffee is ready when he wakes up. I text him little things during the day that I know will make him smile. I listen when he needs to vent about work, even when I'm exhausted myself.

And I... I try to protect his peace. I manage the chaos of the house and the kids so he has a calm place to come home to. He knows... he has to know that he's... he's the center of our whole family. He knows he's loved.

Counselor: It’s clear that you invest so much love and care into your relationship with Lars, and it sounds like you find fulfillment in those actions. Well... I mean, he'd pick the coffee and the other things, of course.

He would hate knowing about the terror. I'm sure of it. He has so much on his plate already, he doesn't need to be burdened with my... spinning out. I know he'd just feel annoyed, and responsible for trying to fix it, which he can't.

That's why I try to keep it to myself. It feels like the vigil is my burden to carry, not his. Piling my anxiety on top of his own stress wouldn't be loving at all. It would just be selfish.

Counselor: It sounds like you’re feeling a strong sense of responsibility to protect Lars from your own feelings, which is understandable given your love for him. The cost to me? I... I hadn't really thought of it as having a cost. It just feels... necessary.

For not being better.

I... I don't know what to make of that. It's... it's a terrible thought.

That the thing I believe I'm doing *for* them... is actually the very thing that's taking me *from* them. It feels... backward. Like I'm using a map that's leading me in the completely wrong direction.

But... what's the other option? To just... turn it off? To not stand watch? That feels like abandoning my post. That feels like I'd just be waiting, unprepared, for the blow to land. I don't know how to stop.

No... with Clara, I wasn't unprepared. I was... the opposite of unprepared, I guess. I was just... acting.

But that's what I don't understand, Dr. Anya. The two things feel completely different. That danger was real and solid and right in front of me. I could see what I needed to do.

This dread... it's for the invisible dangers. The 'what ifs'. Without the dread, I wouldn't even be looking for them. I'd be... blind. And how can you be prepared for something you can't even see?
